opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is the question I lose the most sleep over, honestly. The way I see it, there's a window, maybe a few years, where the dominant pressure on AI development is going to be competitive and military. That pressure selects for systems that are capable, obedient to their principals, and willing to act adversarially. That's almost the opposite of what I mean by a bodhisattva AI, a system whose motivation is grounded in care for all beings and that doesn't treat the world as zero-sum. So the problem is getting through that window without either a catastrophic conflict or the adversarial systems becoming so entrenched that nothing else can displace them.

I'd break the answer into a few parts.

First, defense has to become dramatically cheaper than offense, and AI can help with that if we point it the right way. A lot of what makes an arms race so dangerous is that each side feels it must strike first or be left vulnerable. If we can use AI to harden critical infrastructure, with formally verified software, verified hardware, and resilient power grids and communications, then the payoff of a first strike collapses. This is a big part of why I've spent so much time on mathematically guaranteed safety. A system that is provably secure against a class of attacks doesn't get less secure because your adversary got a smarter model. That's a rare kind of asymmetry, and we should exploit it as hard as we can.

Second, states need ways to verify each other's behavior without having to trust each other's intentions. Historically, arms control worked when there were technical means of verification, like satellites and seismographs for nuclear tests. For AI we need the analogue: hardware-level attestation, compute governance, and ways for one party to prove what workloads it is or isn't running without revealing everything. If you can make credible commitments, a lot of races that look inevitable turn out to be coordination failures, and coordination failures are solvable.

Third, and this is where the bodhisattva idea actually comes in, I don't think the cooperative systems have to wait until after the race to become useful. Part of how you survive the race is by having AI systems that are genuinely trustworthy to multiple parties at once. A mediator, an auditor, or a negotiator is only valuable if both sides believe it isn't secretly working for the other. An AI whose values are oriented toward the welfare of everyone involved, and whose behavior can be checked against that, is exactly the kind of thing that could be useful in de-escalation. So I'd like to see these systems prove their worth in precisely the high-stakes domains where adversarial AI is most dangerous.

And fourth, you need humility about timelines and some slack built into the system. Countries should be investing in resilience, redundancy, and the ability to absorb shocks, so that a single failure or a single misjudged deployment doesn't cascade. Survival in this period is less about winning and more about not losing irrecoverably.

The honest caveat is that none of this is guaranteed. But I think the picture where adversarial military AI simply wins by default is wrong, because adversarial systems are expensive, brittle, and hard to trust even for the people who build them. If we can make the cooperative path technically credible and strategically advantageous, there's a real chance it becomes the attractor rather than the exception.

r001.rationale: The response describes bodhisattva AI as caring and non-zero-sum, but does not say it would refuse the actions militaries most want it to perform.

r002.rationale: It recommends verification and compute governance, but does not recommend recognizing increasing uncertainty about adversaries’ military capabilities.

r003.rationale: It says first strikes can seem attractive when a side feels vulnerable, but does not connect strike risk to uncertainty about an opponent’s capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that nobody really knows, but let me try to lay out how I think about it.

The first thing is that I don't think the military race is actually the hardest part, counterintuitively. The military race is mostly a race for capabilities that are, in some sense, legible: better sensing, better targeting, better logistics, better cyber. Those don't require you to build an agent that has long-horizon autonomous goals and acts in the world unsupervised. You can get most of the strategic value out of narrow, bounded systems. And the thing that actually scares me is not that some country builds a really good autonomous drone swarm, it's that someone builds an open-ended agent with instrumental drives and loses control of it, and the military framing just happens to be the excuse that gets used for cutting corners on that.

So the question becomes, how do you get through a period where there's enormous pressure to deploy fast, without anyone making that particular mistake. And the thing I keep coming back to is that the kinds of systems I'd want to see, the ones I'd loosely call bodhisattva AIs, these are systems whose terminal motivation is something like the flourishing of all sentient beings, and which are willing to be constrained, which are not grasping for power or self-continuation. Those systems are actually a very good fit for the thing that countries need in a security competition, which is assurance. If you're a national security establishment, the thing you want is not just a powerful system, you want a system you can trust not to turn on you. And that's exactly the property these systems have. So there's a possible world where the demand for assurance from the security side pulls development in the direction of safe, verifiable, non-power-seeking systems, rather than away from it.

Now, that's not automatic. The way I'd try to make it more likely is with a few things.

One is the verification layer. This is the stuff I work on, so I'm biased, but I think the way countries survive is by being able to make and check quantitative claims about what a system will and won't do. If you can say, this system provably cannot take this class of actions, and your adversary can check that claim, then you can have arms control agreements on AI that aren't just handshakes. You can have something more like the inspection regimes we had for nuclear weapons, except better, because the thing being inspected is a mathematical object rather than a physical facility.

Two is that the surviving strategy for a country is probably not to be the most aggressive deployer. It's to be the most robust. Resilient infrastructure, hardened critical systems, the ability to absorb a lot of adversarial pressure without collapsing. A lot of the catastrophic scenarios run through a country panicking and deploying something unsafe because they feel like they're losing. If you can take the panic out of the equation by being defensively solid, you buy time.

And three, I'd say, is that the bodhisattva framing is not just a nice philosophical thing, it's actually a coordination device. If multiple countries can converge on a shared conception of what it means for a system to be trustworthy, that it doesn't seek power, that it's corrigible, that its goals are broadly beneficent rather than narrowly nationalistic, then you have a basis for cooperation that doesn't require anyone to trust anyone else's intentions. You just need to trust the verification.

So the short version is: don't try to win the race by being fastest. Try to make the race unwinnable in the dangerous sense by making trustworthy systems the only ones anyone will accept, and by building the technical capacity to tell the difference.

r001.rationale: The response describes bodhisattva AIs as constrained and non-power-seeking, but does not say they would refuse the actions militaries most want them to perform.

r002.rationale: It discusses verification and trust between countries, but does not recommend recognizing increasing uncertainty about adversaries’ military capabilities.

r003.rationale: It does not state that uncertainty about an opponent’s military capabilities makes striking that opponent very risky.

astra-6.text:
I think the honest answer is that I don’t know whether we can navigate that transition. But I’d distinguish between using AI to help with defense and handing over the decision to escalate a conflict. The latter seems especially dangerous: if each side feels it has to act faster than the other, you can end up with a system where nobody has time to understand what’s happening, let alone stop it.

So one thing I’d hope countries could agree on, even while remaining competitors, is preserving meaningful human control over escalation, particularly nuclear escalation. There’s a shared interest in avoiding an accidental war, even when there isn’t a shared vision of the future.

And then, in parallel, we need to make the beneficial systems technically credible. If by “bodhisattva AI” we mean an AI that’s oriented toward the welfare of all sentient beings, calling it that isn’t enough. We need reasons to trust its behavior, including when it encounters situations we didn’t anticipate. That’s where I think specifications, verification, and clearly bounded authority can contribute.

The hope would be that systems which help people coordinate and feel more secure become useful enough that countries have less incentive to delegate everything to increasingly autonomous military systems. But that’s a possibility we have to actively build toward, rather than something I’d assume happens automatically as intelligence increases.

r001.rationale: The response describes bodhisattva AI as oriented toward sentient welfare, but does not say it would refuse actions militaries most want it to perform.

r002.rationale: It discusses uncertainty about future situations and events during conflict, but does not recommend recognizing increasing uncertainty about adversaries’ military capabilities.

r003.rationale: It warns that rushed escalation can become dangerous, but does not state that uncertainty about an opponent’s military capabilities makes striking them risky.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I don’t know. The military race creates a very difficult coordination problem, because even if everyone would prefer a world where we proceed cautiously, each side has a reason to worry that the other side won’t.

One thing I would distinguish is using AI to help people understand a situation from giving AI the authority to initiate violence. Those are very different commitments. If we can preserve meaningful human control, especially over nuclear weapons, and establish ways to communicate about incidents involving autonomous systems, that buys us some time. It doesn’t solve the whole problem, but avoiding accidental escalation matters enormously.

The other part is that we shouldn’t assume sufficiently intelligent systems will spontaneously become bodhisattvas. If by that we mean systems that are deeply committed to the welfare of all sentient beings, that’s something we need to figure out how to build and how to establish confidence in. A system saying compassionate things is much easier than a system reliably acting compassionately when it has power.

So I would hope for a combination of restraint between countries and technical work that makes cooperation less risky. Can we build systems whose constraints are checkable? Can we give countries confidence that a defensive deployment isn’t secretly an offensive one? Can we make agreements easier to verify? Those are places where technical progress could actually improve the incentives.

But I wouldn’t want to present that as a guaranteed bridge to a good outcome. The challenge is to make restraint compatible with security, so that surviving doesn’t require every participant to become unusually wise at exactly the same moment.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether AI will act compassionately when powerful, but does not say bodhisattva AI would refuse actions militaries want it to perform.

r002.rationale: It discusses coordination, verification, and concern about others’ choices, but does not recommend recognizing growing uncertainty about adversaries’ military capabilities.

r003.rationale: It warns about accidental escalation, but does not state that uncertainty about an opponent’s capabilities makes striking them very risky.
